question: An 8-year-old boy presents with a limp favoring his right leg. The patient’s mother noticed he had been limping without complaint for the past 6 months. Past medical history is significant for the flu last year. No current medications. All immunizations are up to date. The vital signs include: temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F), blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg, pulse 74/min, respiratory rate 19/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The body mass index (BMI) is 17.2 kg/m2. On physical examination, the patient is alert and cooperative. A limp favoring the right leg is noted when the patient is walking. There is mild tenderness on deep palpation of the left lumbar region but no erythema, edema, or warmth. There is a decreased range of motion of the left hip. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Limp favoring right leg" -> "Limping for the past 6 months" -> "Decreased range of motion of left hip" -> "Possible Legg-Calve-Perthes disease" -> 70%
CHAIN: "Mild tenderness on deep palpation of left lumbar region" -> "No erythema, edema, or warmth" -> "Possible musculoskeletal origin" -> "Consider Slipped capital femoral epiphysis" -> 60%
CHAIN: "Decreased range of motion of left hip" -> "Limp favoring right leg" -> "Possible Developmental dysplasia of the hip" -> 50%
analysis: The most likely diagnosis in this patient is Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, also known as Perthes disease. This condition typically presents with a limp and decreased range of motion of the hip joint. It commonly affects children between the ages of 4 and 10 years old. The history of limping for several months, tenderness in the hip region, and decreased range of motion are consistent with Legg-Calve-Perthes disease.
